Hmmm...now here's an interesting idea.

The big problem I see is that bash-preexec has to be [the absolute last thing sourced in the shell startup](https://github.com/rcaloras/bash-preexec/issues/97), or else it breaks. This would, in turn, require that we have `starship init` be the last line in the user's shell, and even then, `bash-preexec` will [*still* clobber any existing DEBUG traps](https://github.com/rcaloras/bash-preexec/issues/39).

Fundamentally, I don't think there's a way to avoid clobbering `DEBUG`/`PROMPT_COMMAND` in the bash startup because of the limitations of the shell. We can try to take the edge off of it, but there's simply no way to make it foolproof. In light of that, I think we have two options: we can make a best-effort attempt to compensate ourselves and (possibly noisily) disable modules if that fails, or we can try to provide a framework where the user can provide their own initializations.

I expect this to be  a pretty rare occurrence--the two Bash config frameworks I'm able to find are [Oh-My-Bash](https://github.com/ohmybash/oh-my-bash) and [Bash-it](https://github.com/Bash-it/bash-it). Oh-my-bash doesn't hook `DEBUG` at all, while `Bash-it` only hooks it specifically to provide a `preexec`-like function (sadly, it uses different function names for that functionality than `bash-preexec`).

What I'm taking from above is that it's going to be pretty rare for a user to hook the DEBUG trap without being aware that they've done it, so if we warn them about it, they should usually know how to fix it. We could enhance this by adding something in our documentation if needed.
At this point, I'm thinking we should probably remove Bash support for this feature and circle back to it once we have a robust solution figured out. The rest of the feature seems to work well. 🙂

Unfortunately, it looks like a bug snuck in here. 🐛 
Because we are running the `set` commands before the prompt, we lose the old `$status` to the status code of the `set` command.

It seems we may need to set a variable at the start of the init script to hold onto the `$status` at the time:
```fish
set -l exit_code $status
# ...
starship prompt --status=$exit_code --cmd-duration=$starship_duration;
```

Funnily enough, I fixed that for bash and zsh. I'm not sure whether I missed the fact that it was occurring for fish or just forgot to make the edits.

Is there a way we could do automated tests in an actual shell to catch these sort of regressions? Agreed. We should introduce full end-to-end tests to catch these bugs. 👍
